name: Decoy Effect
description: Adding a third option that is clearly inferior to one existing option (but not the other) increases the choice share of the option it's inferior to, violating rational-choice regularity.
design_relevance_note: The classic 'three pricing tiers where the middle one is designed to look best' pattern.
prevalence_note: Well known specifically in pricing-tier design circles ('the middle option that makes the top one look better'), less universally cited outside that niche.

findings.description: A systematic integrative review spanning four decades of decoy-effect research finds no clear scientific consensus on the underlying mechanism and documents substantial heterogeneity in when and how strongly the effect manifests across contexts — a caution against treating the decoy effect as a uniformly reliable design lever.
findings.source_title: An integrative review of the decoy effect on choice behavior

findings.description: Adding a third 'decoy' option that is asymmetrically dominated by one of two original options (inferior on all attributes) but not the other reliably increases the probability the dominating option is chosen — a systematic violation of the regularity axiom of rational choice.
findings.source_title: Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives: Violations of Regularity and the Similarity Hypothesis

applications.title: YouTube's side-by-side video comparison using a deliberately less attractive option
applications.description: YouTube tested presenting two comparable video recommendations side by side, with one option made deliberately less appealing (fewer views, longer duration, a harder topic) -- making the choice between the two easier by giving the viewer a clear comparison point, the decoy effect's core mechanism.
applications.ethical_note: This nudges a viewer toward a specific video by making the alternative look comparatively worse, which does shape the choice rather than leaving it neutral -- but unlike the decoy-pricing patterns criticized elsewhere in behavioral-economics literature, this doesn't appear to cost the user money or trap them in an unwanted subscription, only steers attention. Graded mixed rather than manipulative_risk given the low stakes of the specific choice being nudged.
